title: What motion design actually is
blurb: What the job is for, before we argue about which software does it.

text.v: Most people arrive at motion design through a piece of software. They see something move, they find out it was made in After Effects, and the first question becomes "how do I learn After Effects".
I think that is the wrong first question, and it costs people about a year.
The job is timing, not tooling
Motion design is deciding what a viewer notices, in what order, and how long they get with each thing. That is the whole job. The software is where you go to write the decision down.

You can tell because the decision survives the tool. A logo that reveals well in After Effects reveals well in Rive, in Blender, in a CSS transition. The timing is the design. Everything else is typing.
This is also why watching a tutorial feels productive and changes nothing. You are watching someone type. The decisions were made before the recording started.
Three things that carry across everything

items.v: Something moves first. Something waits. If everything arrives at once, nothing was emphasised.
How long a thing takes says what it weighs. Slow reads heavy. Fast reads cheap, or urgent, depending on what came before it.
The frames where nothing moves are doing work. Beginners fill them, and the piece turns into noise.

text.v: Learn those three and you can pick up any tool in a fortnight. Learn a tool first and you will make the same piece over and over in it.
So what do you do today
Pick something you already designed. A poster, a logo, a screen. Do not open any software yet.
Write three words for how it should feel. Then write, in plain sentences, what moves first, what waits, and where it rests. Three sentences is enough.
That paragraph is your brief. Every day after this one is about getting better at writing it, and then at hitting it.
Fundamentals are permanent. Tools are exhausting.
